title: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection, acting on analogous variations, has sometimes modified parts in nearly the same way in two distantly related organisms, as with electric organs in unrelated fishes, so that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: so natural selection, working for the good of each being and taking advantage of analogous variations, has sometimes modified in very nearly the same manner two parts in two organic beings, which owe but little of their structure in common to inheritance from the same ancestor.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Cases of difficulty.”. Scope: electric fishes, luminous insects, orchids and Asclepias, and other cases of similar organs in remote groups

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-10: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Convergence is routinely tested with phylogenies, morphology, and molecular data. Existing coverage is strong for canonical examples, though not every similar organ.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place similar organs and their developmental or genetic architectures on independently supported phylogenies and test whether similarity arose on separate branches. Multiple independent origins with convergent function support the claim; homology inherited from one ancestor would refute a proposed case.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Deep homology of regulatory components can coexist with organ-level convergence.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is existential: similar organs have sometimes been built independently. Electric fishes are the stated example, and public genomes, expression studies, and trees already contain the variables needed to separate convergence from homology. A small team can rerun that test in weeks. Other named cases are thinner, but they are not required to confirm or refute the 'sometimes' statement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map electric organs, and the tissues and genes that build them, onto a molecular fish tree. Independent origins from non-homologous muscle or nerve pathways confirm that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor; a single origin with shared developmental identity would refute that reading for this case.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Repeated origins show convergence more cleanly than they show that selection, rather than constraint, produced the similarity.

Luminous insects and the orchid–Asclepias cases are less completely sequenced than electric fishes.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.64
data existence: 0.82
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.78

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Electric organs (Darwin's stated example) occur in fish lineages that are separated on an independently estimated phylogeny by lineages lacking electric organs, so that the organ must have arisen more than once rather than being inherited from one common ancestor; the same holds for light-producing organs in insects (his second example).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The pre-registered family names were resolved with the Open Tree TNRS (exact matches only, context Vertebrates / Arthropods) and an induced subtree of the synthetic tree was requested for the matched ott ids. Taxa pruned from the synthesis (Lamnidae) or non-monophyletic in it and mapped to an internal node already containing other sampled tips were dropped; the rest were coded 1 (electric / luminous) or 0 (background). Unary node chains were collapsed, then the number of maximal all-1 clades (Dollo minimum number of independent origins) and the Fitch parsimony minimum number of state changes were computed on the induced tree.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: on the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on a fixed list of electric-organ-bearing fish families and a fixed list of non-electric fish families, count (i) the Dollo minimum number of independent origins = number of maximal clades whose tips are all electric, and (ii) the Fitch parsimony minimum number of state changes. SUPPORTS if, for the electric-fish case, (i) >= 3 and (ii) >= 3 (no reconstruction with a single origin and fewer than three changes exists). The insect light-organ case is scored the same way and reported; it does not decide the verdict because the claim is existential ('has sometimes').

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the electric-organ-bearing families form a single clade in the synthetic tree (Dollo origins = 1, Fitch changes = 1). MIXED if Dollo origins = 2, or if the two statistics disagree about whether >= 3 changes are needed. If the Open Tree API is unreachable or fewer than 80% of the listed families map to the tree, the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: minimum independent origins (Dollo) of electric organs among fish families on the Open Tree synthetic tree

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: Fitch parsimony minimum changes = 6; 10 electric tips of 45

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's claim has two parts: that similar organs sometimes arose independently in distantly related organisms (testable from a phylogeny) and that natural selection acting on analogous variations produced them (a mechanism not tested here). Only the first, pattern part is tested. 'Electric organs of fishes' = the families with electrogenic organs in the modern literature: Torpedinidae, Narcinidae, Narkidae, Hypnidae (Torpediniformes), Rajidae (skates), Mormyridae and Gymnarchidae (Mormyroidea), Gymnotidae, Apteronotidae, Sternopygidae, Hypopomidae, Rhamphichthyidae (Gymnotiformes), Malapteruridae (electric catfish) and Uranoscopidae (stargazers); Darwin knew Torpedo, Gymnotus and the electric catfish. 'Luminous organs of insects' = Lampyridae, Phengodidae, Rhagophthalmidae, Elateridae (Pyrophorini), Keroplatidae (Arachnocampa, Orfelia). 'Independently estimated phylogeny' = the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree, whose fish and insect backbones derive mostly from molecular studies. Independence is counted on a tree whose tips are families; origins within a family are not counted separately, which makes the count conservative.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Open Tree of Life synthetic tree opentree16.1 (taxonomy 3.7draft3) via the v3 API: tnrs/match_names and tree_of_life/induced_subtree

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The six electric clades recovered (Torpediniformes, Rajidae, Mormyroidea, Gymnotiformes, Malapteruridae, Uranoscopidae) are separated by many non-electric families, so the result is insensitive to the exact background sample; it also matches the count in the modern literature, which was not used as input.

Only the pattern half of the claim (independent origins) is tested; whether natural selection on 'analogous variations' produced them is not addressed by a phylogeny.

Seven of 52 fish names (Narcinidae, Gymnotidae, Sternopygidae, Hypopomidae, Rhinobatidae, Serranidae, Lamnidae) could not be placed as tips because they are non-monophyletic in the synthetic tree or pruned from it; every dropped electric family belongs to a clade (Torpediniformes, Gymnotiformes) that is already represented, so the count is unchanged.

The luminous-insect case gives 2 independent origins (Lampyridae + Rhagophthalmidae; Keroplatidae) because Elateridae and Phengodidae could not be placed as tips; the literature count is higher. It was pre-registered as reported-only.

The synthetic tree is a supertree whose fish backbone comes mostly from molecular studies; it carries no branch support, so no uncertainty on the origin count is given.
